headline: Malaysia's new rules make firms vet their algorithms. The state's own are exempt.
context: On 30 April 2026 the data-protection regulator issued Malaysia's first rules on automated profiling, making firms vet any system that profiles people. The rules rest on a 2010 law that exempts the Federal and State Governments, which the minister says was built for commercial dealings.

cards.big: On 30 April Malaysia issued its first rules forcing any firm that profiles you to run an impact check. The one profiler they cannot reach is the Federal and State Governments.
cards.sub: Section 3 of that 2010 law carves both out. PADU, the state database on 30.7 million people, falls outside it.

cards.big: After 22.5 million Malaysians' MyKad details were put up for sale in 2022, the data-protection law gave no remedy against a government agency, whoever leaked them.
cards.sub: Section 3 says the Act 'shall not apply to the Federal Government and State Governments.' The minister denied it came from the registration department.

cards.big: Any firm that profiles people by machine must now run an impact assessment, even on one person. PADU holds 30.7 million socio-economic profiles, and is exempt.
cards.sub: Since May 2026 PADU runs predictive analytics for 26 agencies, scoring who can repay a government loan. No law makes it run that check.

cards.big: The carve-out is no oversight: a 2020 review weighed extending the Act to the government, and the 2024 reform still left Section 3 untouched.
cards.sub: Two newer laws guard state data from hackers and jail officers who leak it. Neither lets a citizen see, question, or refuse how a government system profiled them.

cards.big: The government now demands of every business an amanah it refuses to place on itself.
It reads like a fire code every shop must follow, while the largest building in town, the one the council owns, is written out of the rules.
cards.sub: Private firms must vet their profiling systems. PADU and other government databases need not.

cards.big: Malaysia wrote rules to hold algorithms accountable to people, then exempted the algorithms that decide who gets help, who gets flagged, and who gets missed.

revisions: REPHRASED (Stage 2 bias): fact-Technology sub 'clears every threshold and answers to none of them' → 'clears every threshold; the Act that sets them cannot bind it' — scopes the claim to the data-protection Act so it cannot be misread as 'subject to no rules at all' (internal directives and the Cyber Security Act 2024 exist, but grant no data-subject recourse).

REPHRASED (Stage 2 bias): added the government's stated rationale to the context ('on the basis it governs commercial dealings') so the exemption's official justification is visible, per the omission flag.

CORRECTED (Stage 3): PADU figure changed from '30.7 million' to 'more than 30 million' to reconcile The Edge's 30.7m with T4A's own published issue 1102 ('30.4 million profiles by June 2025'); 'more than 30 million' is true under both and avoids false precision and an internal corpus inconsistency.

REPHRASED (Stage 3 conservatism): fact-Governance big 'the Cabinet rejected a proposal' → 'a proposal to delete Section 3 was rejected' — the 'Cabinet' attribution is single-sourced and second-hand (FMT); the retention in the 2024 Act independently supports 'left it standing'.

INTRODUCED (Stage 6 self-verified): reframe rewritten from the validator-flagged 'The question is not X, it is Y' template to a hard declarative ('The government now demands of every business an amanah it refuses to place on itself'). Verified: the asymmetry (private-sector DPIA duty vs s.3 government exemption) traces to Act 709 s.3 and the JPDP DPIA guideline. 'amanah' (Malay/Arabic: fiduciary trust) is the single elevated word.
INTRODUCED (Stage 6 self-verified): hook/fact-1 lengths trimmed to keep big+sub within the ~300 combined cap; no factual content dropped (verified each trimmed line still traces to s.1/s.3 sources).

CORRECTED (external deep-research report, primary-verified): fact-Governance sub 'Singapore... Malaysia passed no equivalent' was factually wrong. Malaysia HAS public-sector data statutes — Cyber Security Act 2024 (Act 854, in force 26 Aug 2024) and Data Sharing Act 2025 (Act 864, in force 28 Apr 2025; s.18 RM1m/5y officer penalty, verified jdn.gov.my/nacsa.gov.my). Rewrote to the accurate gap: those laws guard data security and punish leaking officers, but none grants a citizen an algorithmic-accountability right. Singapore dropped from the card (it also exempts its public sector and uses internal AI governance, so it is not a clean foil).

STRENGTHENED (external deep-research report, primary-verified): fact-Technology sub now carries PADU's May 2026 'Analytics-as-a-Service' pivot (26 agencies; scoring loan-repayment capability) instead of restating the threshold numbers — establishes PADU as an ACTIVE automated-profiling engine, not a static database, closing the 'PADU is just storage' rebuttal. Verified The Star/Malay Mail/FMT 20 Apr 2026.

CORRECTED (primary-verified): PADU figure set to '30.7 million' (current April 2026 figure, multiply-sourced incl. SAYS/Malay Mail/FMT) — distinct date from issue 1102's 30.4m (Jun 2025), so no contradiction; chose the concrete current number over 'more than 30 million'.

REPHRASED (overclaim guard): view 'who gets watched' to 'who gets flagged' — PADU's documented function is subsidy/loan/welfare targeting (incl. loan-repayment flagging), not surveillance; 'flagged' avoids a surveillance overclaim and is supported by the repayment-scoring use case.

CORRECTED (Stage 3, external ChatGPT): 'adopted' to 'issued' (hook + context) — the guideline PDFs say 'issued'; the 30 April date is a launch (JPDP X post + reporting), not an 'adoption' stamped on the texts.

CORRECTED (Stage 3, external ChatGPT): fact-Technology 'file an impact assessment' to 'run an impact assessment' — ADMP triggers carrying OUT a DPIA regardless of volume, but no primary duty to FILE/submit every DPIA to the Commissioner (submission only on high residual risk).

CORRECTED (Stage 3, external ChatGPT): dropped '600+ data points' — not traceable to a PADU/Economy Ministry primary document (only secondary reporting). Kept the primary-verified '30.7 million socio-economic profiles' (official PADU material, 20 Apr 2026).

CORRECTED (Stage 3, external ChatGPT): fact-Rights reframed with 'whoever leaked them' — the 2022 breach origin was disputed (minister denied NRD), so the no-remedy point is now stated as the general statutory consequence rather than implying a specific government agency caused the leak. PADU stays squarely exempt (run by the Ministry of Economy, a federal body).

Per the stage6-preamble over-integration rule, a verified-accurate point is not averaged away to reduce rhetorical contrast. Kept.

No card claims ALL public bodies are exempt; the bite-size budget does not permit a statutory-body caveat, and the named profiler (PADU) is squarely within the exemption. Logged, not actioned.

View card flagged UNVERIFIED/opinion: the 'considered view' card is explicitly editorial synthesis. 'who gets help / flagged / missed' is now grounded in PADU's verified use cases (subsidy eligibility; loan-repayment scoring; targeting that can miss people). Retained as labelled editorial synthesis, not a factual claim.

introduced_claims.claim: The private-sector DPIA/profiling duty and the s.3 government exemption are the two sides of one asymmetry (reframe).
introduced_claims.source: Act 709 s.3 (exemption) + JPDP DPIA Guideline 30 Apr 2026 (any-profiling trigger). Both in brief S1/S3.

synthesis_notes: No over-integration conflicts: Stage 2 (soften the 'answers to none' line) and Stage 3 (keep alleged/denied 2022 framing; soften 'Cabinet') pointed the same direction, toward conservatism, and both were applied without averaging away the core asymmetry. The load-bearing claim — that the new accountability regime binds the private sector while the state's own profiling sits outside the Act — survives every fix intact because it is statutory, not interpretive. Compression preserved every qualifier: 'put up for sale' (not 'leaked by'), 'denied it came from', 'a proposal ... was rejected', 'more than 30 million'. Dominant hook emotion: anxiety-of-precedent / anger-at-process (the rule-maker exempts itself), not sadness. Reframe rotated off the flagged template family. One elevated word only ('amanah').
sr_score_rationale: Clean synthesis: a statutory spine that no fix could dislodge, two bias/accuracy softenings applied without diluting the finding, an internal-corpus number reconciliation (vs issue 1102), and a reframe rotated off the drift template while keeping the single elevated word. Held at 86, not higher, because two specifics (exact DPIA thresholds; the 'v1.0/adopted' wording) still rest on advisories pending confirmation against the published guideline PDFs, and the external Gemini/ChatGPT cross-checks remain to be run before going live to main.
